newsitem.title: FRANCE: Franc drops to two-month low on EMU jitters.
newsitem.headline: Franc drops to two-month low on EMU jitters.

text.p: Doubts about France's commitment to a single currency knocked the franc to a two-month low against the German mark on Thursday as efforts by France and Germany to reassure the markets appeared to fail.

Calls from leading French politicians for a devaluation of the franc, rumours of a government reshuffle, a tough truckers' strike and France's inability to get its economy going were to blame for the volatility on the currency market, analysts said.
France and Germany did their best to calm the jitters, reaffirming their commitment to qualify on time for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999.

In a joint statement, French Prime Minister Alain Juppe and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said they had reaffirmed in a telephone conversation on Thursday that the current franc-mark rate was in line with economic fundamentals.

"They reaffirmed the commitment of France and Germany to launch Economic and Monetary Union within the timetable and convergence criteria fixed by the (Maastricht) treaty," the statement, released in both Paris and Bonn, said.
Bank of France monetary policy council member Jean Boissonnat weighed in with his own currency support, saying the franc was probably slightly undervalued against the mark.
"The franc is in an excellent competitive situation compared to the mark. We are probably even slightly undervalued compared to the mark," he told French radio.
But their efforts were not enough to prevent the franc dropping nearly a full centime during the day to trade at 3.3924 per mark at 1705 GMT, down from 3.3829 on Wednesday.
Analysts said the leaders had little choice but to try to shore up the currency.

"You just sense that there is so much popular discontent and opposition discontent with the 'franc fort' policy that they had to make a strong response," Nomura International market strategist Sonja Gibbs said.

Gibbs and other analysts said the Franco-German statement was a direct response to a call by former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing for a weaker franc and was meant to reassure markets that they would not abandon their push for EMU.
"It shows they are denying all rumours of a change in direction or policy," said Cyril Beuzit, bond strategist at Banque Nationale de Paris.
Although Giscard d'Estaing later denied in Bonn he was calling for a devaluation of the franc against the mark. He said, however, a stronger dollar would be useful for the French economy.

His earlier comments were interpreted by the market as implying a need for the franc to also fall against the mark, fuelling a debate about the usually-taboo subject of the franc-mark exchange rate and France's commitment to monetary union.
His comments were not the franc's only problem, and traditional opponents of monetary union piled into the debate.

"Valery Giscard d'Estaing has hit the nail on the head by stating that employment is the absolute priority," Gaullist National Assembly speaker and former anti-Maastricht campaigner Philippe Seguin said on Thursday.
Despite repeated denials, persistent rumours of a near-term cabinet reshuffle, have also plagued the markets recently.
And a four-day strike by truckers blocking roads and barricading fuel depots across France raised fears that social unrest could take hold in a repeat of 1995's paralysing strikes.
